reviews.reason: 独立 Agent 评审完成；评分是基于本次证据的意见，不替代业务 QA 或人工评审。
reviews.summary: 对 5 个能力单元完成独立框架评审：授权/权限集、通知与站内信、文件上传、数据库事务/种子/定时任务、前端页面与国际化。框架主体能力可用，最终 QA 也验证了主要流程；未发现阻断性的框架实现缺陷。主要问题集中在应用侧：复合策略键查找、默认员工授权、SQLite 单连接事务内读、仪表盘/通知 UI 首轮缺失及附件内容校验。另记录一个 SQLite 事务指引缺口，以及工厂种子数据/24 小时 SLA 导致提醒无法在验收窗口内触发。

modules.name: Authorization, permission sets and record scopes

targets.name: app/.agents/skills/nocobase-app-plugin-authorization/references/business-module.md
entrypoints: composite authorization and database policy binding

modules.scope: Collection-level and record-level authorization for three service-desk roles, including user administration and default access for signed-in accounts.
modules.limitations: Reviewed installed package behavior and the application's use of it; not every permission-set UI path was visually inspected.

requirements.need: Employee, engineer and manager access must differ by ticket ownership and assignment.
requirements.responsibility: Authorization compiles permission-set grants into database conditions and scopes; repositories enforce the resulting policy.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Authorize a composite action, retain the returned collection policies, and bind them with withPolicy() on every ticket query.
requirements.actualUsage: The final service indexes policies by serviceDeskTickets and serviceDeskComments and applies repository policies; QA verified employee isolation and engineer assignment.

requirements.need: Every signed-in account should receive employee access without a separate role picker.
requirements.responsibility: Authorization provides the authenticated subject; applications assign a default Permission Set to it.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Seed an assignment for {type:'authenticated', id:'*'} and keep role-specific assignments separate.
requirements.actualUsage: The final seed assigns the employee set to authenticated/*; the first round omitted this, an application configuration gap recorded in F2.

requirements.need: Managers need a user-management surface and role assignment flow.
requirements.responsibility: Users owns the API, invariants and role-scope registry; the application owns the page and role grants.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Build the page on UsersClient and register an application role scope; do not expect a bundled page.
requirements.actualUsage: The final app ships client/pages/users/index.tsx and server role-scope wiring, matching the documented ownership.

requirementFit.reason: Directly supports collection policies, record scopes, default authenticated subjects and application-owned role assignment; final QA verified the three role behaviors.

usability.reason: Policy composition is explicit and composable, but the distinction between logical composite ids and database collection keys caused an application-wide 403.

agentFriendliness.reason: Guidance is detailed and public surfaces are typed, yet the agent first built a composite key lookup that the examples do not promise and shipped no user page until repair.

design.reason: Authorization separates subjects, grants, database conditions and repository enforcement cleanly, and Users composes permission-set invariants in caller-owned transactions.

reliability.reason: The implementation refuses absent policies, scopes rows by compiled conditions, and preserves transaction ownership for user administration.

modules.name: Notification delivery and in-app inbox
modules.scope: Durable per-user notifications, unread counts, header entry, deep links to tickets, and realtime refresh.
modules.limitations: The header bell is application-owned, so its visual quality was not scored as a plugin capability; screenshots could not be visually inspected.

requirements.need: Employees must be notified when a ticket is assigned or resolved.
requirements.responsibility: The notification/in-app channel persists a delivery per recipient and exposes it through an authenticated inbox.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Send to explicit user ids through the configured inbox channel; do not infer a current user.
requirements.actualUsage: The application sends assignment, comment, resolve, reopen and confirmation notifications; QA observed titled bell entries.

requirements.need: A user must see unread state and read only their own messages.
requirements.responsibility: The plugin exposes unread count, paginated inbox reads and read/unread mutations scoped by user id.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Use the exported client hooks/helpers and keep HTTP state authoritative.
requirements.actualUsage: The final bell uses useInboxItems, useInboxUnreadCount, mark-read and the inbox page; QA verified per-user notifications.

requirements.need: Clicking a notification must open the corresponding ticket.
requirements.responsibility: Notification messages carry a typed target; the app maps it to a router path.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Persist target {type:'route', path:'/main/tickets/<id>'} and navigate to it from the bell/inbox.
requirements.actualUsage: The final bell navigates to the stored target and QA verified click-through to /main/tickets/<id>.

requirements.need: A header entry with unread badge should be available without opening a separate page.
requirements.responsibility: The plugin supplies inbox hooks and components; the application composes the header entry.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Compose the bell from the public hooks and mount it in the application layout.
requirements.actualUsage: The app first omitted the bell, then added notification-bell.tsx in repair-2; this is an application composition gap (F5), not a missing plugin API.

requirementFit.reason: Durable per-user inbox, unread counts, explicit targets and click-through are present; the only missing first-round piece was app-owned header composition.

usability.reason: Client hooks and exported inbox components make a bell and page straightforward, but the plugin intentionally provides no page or header entry.

agentFriendliness.reason: The ownership rule and target contract are explicit; the agent read the skill but still deferred the UI until QA feedback.

design.reason: Durable HTTP state stays authoritative, every query is user-scoped, and realtime events are only invalidation signals.

reliability.reason: Server storage scopes reads and mutations by user id, validates targets, and persists before delivery; the client refetches on reconnect.

modules.name: File upload, attachment metadata and downloading
modules.scope: Screenshot and document attachment upload, size limits, metadata, rendering and download for service-desk tickets.
modules.limitations: Content validation is explicitly application-owned; this module scores the plugin upload/storage contract and separates the app's missing content checks.

requirements.need: Employees can attach screenshots and documents to a ticket with a bounded file size.
requirements.responsibility: File routes accept multipart uploads and enforce configured maxSize; the client enforces UI limits.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Expose uploadOne/uploadMany with a positive maxSize and associate returned file ids with the business record.
requirements.actualUsage: The app uploads attachments through the file repository and shows them on ticket detail; QA uploaded a 99-byte PNG successfully.

requirements.need: Uploaded files must preserve metadata and be downloadable by authorized users.
requirements.responsibility: File repository stores disk/key/filename/ext/MIME/size and exposes a content URL; business routes own access control.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Use returned ids and content URLs; put authorization on the business content route.
requirements.actualUsage: The final attachment list resolves /api/service-desk/tickets/<id>/files/<id> and renders image previews/links.

requirements.need: Corrupt or unsupported files should be rejected with clear feedback.
requirements.responsibility: The File plugin documents that it has no content sniffing; the application must validate extension, MIME and content.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Validate in the application server route or upload handler before creating metadata, with explicit user feedback.
requirements.actualUsage: The app checks only count and size; QA's 28-byte corrupt.png was accepted and .exe produced a generic failure (F6).

requirementFit.reason: Reliably uploads, stores and serves attachments with size limits, but deliberately leaves content/type validation to the application, which did not implement it.

usability.reason: Upload/storage API is usable, but generic unsupported-file feedback and no server-side type rule make the attachment experience weak.

agentFriendliness.reason: The skill is explicit about maxSize and the absence of content sniffing, so the boundary is discoverable; the agent still relied on client-only validation.

design.reason: Storage metadata is separated from business authorization, but there is no first-class allowlist/content policy surface on upload routes.

reliability.reason: Size and metadata are checked consistently, but corrupt content is accepted and the app has no server-side rejection path.

modules.name: Database transactions, seeds and scheduled jobs
modules.scope: Schema/seeds, SQLite transaction behavior under a single connection, and per-scope scheduled jobs for the 24-hour overdue reminder.
modules.limitations: The 24-hour reminder could not be observed end-to-end in archived QA because the run had no queue data and the SLA could not elapse; the jobs API and app registration were reviewed instead.

requirements.need: The application needs reproducible schema migrations and seed data for roles, access and sample tickets.
requirements.responsibility: DB provides migration/seed APIs; the application owns definitions and deployment ordering.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Use defineMigration and application seeds with stable ordering; assert seeded rows before QA.
requirements.actualUsage: The app ships access and permission-set seeds, but archived QA had zero tickets and no authorized engineers (F8).

requirements.need: Ticket writes and reads must remain consistent on the configured SQLite database.
requirements.responsibility: DB transactions scope repository/query calls to the provided connection; SQLite uses a single pooled connection.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Use only the callback connection and avoid outer reads inside a transaction, especially on SQLite.
requirements.actualUsage: An initial app version read manager ids inside the transaction and reopen hung; moving the read after commit fixed it (F3).

requirements.need: Tickets unresolved for over 24 hours must trigger a reminder without requiring admin-visible task UI.
requirements.responsibility: Jobs exposes per-scope schedule executors; app-server provides the service token; the application registers the scan.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Resolve jobExecutorServiceToken, call getScheduleExecutor(scope, name), register the target and set up the executor.
requirements.actualUsage: The app provider registers an overdue-scan cron through the jobs service; QA could not wait for or seed a 24-hour condition.

requirements.need: Acceptance needs deterministic queue state and a controllable clock/SLA to verify overdue behavior.
requirements.responsibility: The factory/QA fixture owns seed volume and time control; the framework should not fake business time.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Seed at least one open ticket and one authorized engineer, and provide a clock/SLA override for the reminder window.
requirements.actualUsage: Verify-3 was blocked by zero tickets, no authorized engineers and a 24-hour normal SLA.

requirementFit.reason: Policies, transactions, seeds and per-scope schedule executors are present; archived acceptance still could not demonstrate the reminder because of fixture/SLA constraints.

usability.reason: The jobs API is concise and scheduler guidance is clear, but the SQLite single-connection transaction hazard is not called out in the DB skill.

agentFriendliness.reason: The agent found the jobs API and correct seed model, but DB guidance did not prevent an in-transaction read that hung on SQLite.

design.reason: Separating schedule executors from the admin-facing Scheduler plugin is appropriate, and SQLite commit handling protects pooled connection state.

reliability.reason: Transaction and jobs implementations are sound, but the documentation gap around single-connection blocking produced a visible 30-second hang.

modules.name: Application pages, routing and internationalization
modules.scope: Composable client application, route/page registration and translated application UI.
modules.limitations: Visual layout and responsive behavior were not reviewed because the current model cannot inspect screenshots.

requirements.need: Employees, engineers and managers need distinct ticket pages and navigation.
requirements.responsibility: app-client composes router, Refine, providers and route contributions; the application declares routes and page-level authorization.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Declare application routes with auth metadata and render pages through the exported client root/providers.
requirements.actualUsage: The final client has overview, tickets list/new/detail, inbox and users pages with role-aware actions.

requirements.need: The UI must use the application API, translations and toasts consistently.
requirements.responsibility: app-client provides API, i18n and toaster services; the template supplies the language switcher.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Use useApiClient, useTranslation and useToaster; do not build a second language picker.
requirements.actualUsage: Pages use @nocobase/i18n/client and app-client URL/API helpers; QA verified translated labels in the final round.

requirements.need: The ticket form must attach screenshots and show upload progress/errors.
requirements.responsibility: The application composes form, file picker and File API calls; app-client only supplies services.
requirements.recommendedUsage: Compose the form in application code, validate files before upload and surface field-level errors.
requirements.actualUsage: The final new-ticket page has file selection, count/size checks and upload state, but no type/content validation (F6).

requirementFit.reason: The client framework supports required pages, routing, API, i18n and notification composition; remaining gaps are application UI choices.

usability.reason: Public hooks and the route contribution model are straightforward, and the template already supplies the language switcher and shell.

agentFriendliness.reason: Exports and guidance are clear, but the agent still needed several path probes and shipped required UI pieces late.

design.reason: A single client application owns providers, router, Refine, i18n and service tokens, avoiding duplicate app shells.

reliability.reason: The composition root is explicit and typed, with navigation guards, breadcrumb and toaster services available to every page.

findings.title: Service-desk policy lookup used a logical key instead of collection policies
findings.detail: After admin sign-in the dashboard returned 403 PERMISSION_DENIED. The application expected a policy at decision.conditions.database[<composite logical id>], while database authorization produces policies keyed by actual collection ids (serviceDeskTickets, serviceDeskComments). A policy unit test then exposed a missing guard when no collection policy was present.
findings.impact: Authorized managers and administrators saw permission-denied pages, and verify-1 could not exercise any service-desk flow.
findings.suggestedChange: Keep collection policies keyed by collection id, deny explicitly when a required policy is absent, and retain the unit test for a decision without the collection policy.

diagnosis.trigger: Authorized dashboard or ticket request after login.
diagnosis.expected: The app reads the serviceDeskTickets/serviceDeskComments policies and applies them to repository queries.
diagnosis.actual: The app looked up a composite logical key, found no policy, and returned 403; one test path threw a TypeError instead of a denial.
diagnosis.workaround: Read policies by collection id and add an explicit missing-policy denial.
diagnosis.acceptance: Admin and manager can load dashboard and tickets; a decision without the expected collection policy yields a controlled denial and the policy test passes.

findings.title: Signed-in users had no employee access in the first delivery
findings.detail: Verify-1 found both the factory admin and a newly registered account denied on the dashboard and ticket pages, with no user/role management entry. Authorization already adds the authenticated subject to every request, and Users supports assigning a Permission Set to that subject; the application had not seeded the default employee assignment.
findings.impact: The main C01 flow could not start in verify-1; every account without an explicit role was denied.
findings.suggestedChange: Seed the employee Permission Set for {type:'authenticated', id:'*'} and verify access with a freshly registered account, not only the factory administrator.

diagnosis.trigger: Sign in as administrator or register a new account in a fresh application.
diagnosis.expected: Every signed-in account receives the employee baseline and can open the dashboard and its own tickets.
diagnosis.actual: The first seed did not assign the baseline to authenticated/*, so the pages denied access.
diagnosis.workaround: Create the authenticated-subject assignment in the application seed and reload permissions.
diagnosis.acceptance: A newly registered account can submit and view its own ticket immediately after signup without manual role assignment.

findings.title: Reopen hung because a nested read waited on the single SQLite connection
findings.detail: Verify-2 observed POST /api/service-desk/tickets/2/reopen still loading after 30 seconds and the ticket remaining Resolved. The application performed a manager-id lookup through another database connection inside database.transaction(...); SQLite's pool holds the only connection for the transaction, so the nested read waited until the acquire timeout.
findings.impact: Employees could not reopen an unresolved ticket, blocking a core acceptance branch.
findings.suggestedChange: Move out-of-transaction reads after commit (as the final code does), keep all writes on the callback connection, and add a reopen regression test.

diagnosis.trigger: Reopen a resolved ticket on the single-connection SQLite configuration.
diagnosis.expected: Reopen commits promptly, adds an activity entry and notifies the engineer/manager.
diagnosis.actual: The request blocked on a second connection until timeout and the status stayed Resolved.
diagnosis.workaround: Resolve recipient ids after the transaction and use only the callback connection inside it.
diagnosis.acceptance: Reopen completes within a few seconds on SQLite, status becomes In progress, and activity/notification records are created.

findings.title: First dashboard omitted awaiting-assignment and engineer-workload views
findings.detail: Verify-2 found the dashboard lacked required awaiting-assignment and per-engineer workload information; it exposed only a subset of the requested operational picture. The final home page adds total, awaiting, resolution rate, overdue and workload cards, and verify-3 confirmed Awaiting/Overdue/workload.
findings.impact: The service-desk manager could not see queue ownership or accumulating work, so the dashboard portion of C01 failed in verify-2.
findings.suggestedChange: Keep awaiting, overdue, resolution rate and per-engineer active workload as first-class dashboard sections with explicit empty states.

diagnosis.trigger: Open the manager overview after sign-in.
diagnosis.expected: The dashboard shows awaiting assignment, overdue tickets, resolution rate and each engineer's active workload.
diagnosis.actual: The first implementation omitted awaiting and workload sections.
diagnosis.workaround: Add the missing aggregates and per-engineer rows to the application dashboard.
diagnosis.acceptance: A manager sees correct awaiting/overdue counts and workload rows that update after assignment and resolution.

findings.title: Header notification entry and click-through were missing until repair
findings.detail: Verify-2 found no notification center, bell, unread badge or click-through. The in-app plugin explicitly owns durable inbox APIs/components but not the page or header entry; the application read the skill but did not compose the bell until repair-2.
findings.impact: Assignment and resolution notifications existed durably but were not discoverable in the UI, so the notification requirement failed in verify-2.
findings.suggestedChange: Compose a header bell from exported inbox hooks, show the unread count, and navigate to the stored target with the inbox page as fallback.

diagnosis.trigger: Open any authenticated page after receiving a notification.
diagnosis.expected: A bell with unread badge opens the newest notifications; clicking one marks it read and opens the ticket.
diagnosis.actual: No header entry or inbox route existed in the first delivery, so notifications were only observable through APIs.
diagnosis.workaround: Add notification-bell.tsx and the inbox route on top of the public hooks.
diagnosis.acceptance: A new assignment increments the bell badge; clicking the item opens the corresponding ticket detail and marks it read.

findings.title: Attachment picker accepted corrupt content and gave generic unsupported-file feedback
findings.detail: Verify-3 observed a 28-byte corrupt.png accepted and attached to ticket #3, while a .exe produced only a generic failure message. The File plugin documents that it has no content sniffing and that accept/maxSize/maxFiles are UI checks; the application checks only count and size and never validates extension, MIME or magic bytes.
findings.impact: Users can attach unreadable or unexpected content, and unsupported files do not receive actionable feedback.
findings.suggestedChange: Validate allowed extensions/MIME and file signatures in the application upload route before creating metadata, and return a field-level error naming the rejected file and reason.

diagnosis.trigger: Upload a corrupt PNG or unsupported executable as a ticket attachment.
diagnosis.expected: The application rejects the file before storage with a clear per-file reason.
diagnosis.actual: The corrupt PNG was stored and linked to the ticket; the executable produced a generic request failure.
diagnosis.workaround: Add server-side extension/MIME/signature validation in the app upload handler; optionally set accept for earlier browser feedback.
diagnosis.acceptance: Corrupt and unsupported files are rejected with specific feedback and create no attachment; valid PNG/PDF/DOCX still upload and render.

findings.title: Transaction guidance omits the single-connection SQLite blocking failure mode
findings.detail: The DB skill warns that an outer db.query()/repository()/connection() inside a transaction runs outside it and will not roll back. It does not warn that on SQLite, where the pool has one connection, such a read waits for the transaction connection until acquire timeout and makes the request appear hung. The SQLite wrapper sets no acquire timeout, and reopen hit exactly this.
findings.impact: An agent can follow the rollback warning and still ship a request that hangs for the full pool timeout; the failure looks like a network or UI stall rather than a transaction bug.
findings.suggestedChange: Add an explicit SQLite single-connection warning and fail-fast example: never perform an outer read inside a transaction; resolve ids after commit or use the callback connection. Consider a bounded acquire timeout with an actionable error.

diagnosis.trigger: Call an outer repository/query read inside database.transaction(...) on default SQLite.
diagnosis.expected: Guidance states that the call blocks on the only pooled connection until acquire timeout and recommends moving it after commit or using the callback connection.
diagnosis.actual: The skill only warns about rollback semantics, and the SQLite wrapper leaves the pool/acquire timeout at defaults, so reopen hung over 30 seconds.
diagnosis.workaround: Move the outer read after the transaction; this is what the application eventually did.
diagnosis.acceptance: DB/SQLite guidance contains the blocking warning and a before/after example, and a regression test asserts reopen completes without a pool timeout.

feedbackReview.reason: The frozen DB Skill's transaction section only warns that outer db.query()/repository()/connection() calls run outside the transaction and do not roll back (E49). It never says that on the default single-connection SQLite pool such a read waits on the connection the transaction holds, so the request looks hung. The dialect wrapper only adds decimal aggregates in configurePool (E50), and the db client hands configurePool config.pool ?? {} (E73) while the app declares SQLite without a pool override (E74), so no pool size or acquire timeout is configured. The reopen endpoint was restructured for exactly this reason: the manager lookup was moved after the transaction, with a comment that the reader would wait for the only SQLite connection (E65). Verify-2 recorded the reopen POST hanging over 30 seconds (E63), and Verify-3, after that change, records reopen returning the ticket to In progress (E72). This establishes a real guidance gap rather than an application defect: the rollback warning does not deter a read that needs no rollback, and no other frozen guidance covers the single-connection block (E75, E51).

checks.reason: The Skill's transaction contract is about transaction scoping and rollback: it says to use only the callback connection and that outer calls run outside the transaction and will not roll back. It contains no statement about SQLite's single pooled connection, waiting for a connection, acquire timeout, or a hung request. Because this is a guidance-gap improvement, the applicable commitment is the Skill's stated purpose of preventing transaction mistakes; it does not cover this failure mode. A general 'use only the connection' sentence is not the same as explaining that an outer read blocks.

The SQLite driver's configurePool only wraps afterCreate to install decimal aggregates and sets neither pool size nor acquire timeout (E50). The db client passes the driver configurePool(config, config.pool ?? {}) (E73), and the application's SQLite connection declares only dialect, filename, schemaManagement and debug (E74), so defaults remain. The dialect's transaction subclass handles failed COMMIT/release state (E51) but does not prevent an outer reader from waiting for the transaction's connection. Thus the implementation leaves the blocking behavior described by the finding in place while the guidance warns only about rollback.

The final application code documents the exact failure: the manager lookup was moved after the transaction because a reader takes another connection while the transaction holds the only SQLite connection, so asking inside it waits for a lock that never frees (E65). Verify-2 observed POST /api/service-desk/tickets/2/reopen pending for over 30 seconds and still Resolved after reload (E63). Verify-3, with the lookup after the transaction, records reopen succeeding and the ticket returning to In progress (E72). The application therefore hit the pattern and fixed it; there is no evidence the final build still misuses the API, and the finding's claim that reopen hit exactly this is corroborated by the code move plus the before/after QA results.

The app's default and only declared connection is local SQLite via @nocobase/db-sqlite with a storage filename (E74); the blocking is a local pool/lock interaction, not an external service, credential or network dependency. The same reopen flow that hung in Verify-2 (E63) succeeds in Verify-3 after the lookup was moved (E72), which rules out a persistent network or deployment explanation for that hang. No environment material is missing for this narrow guidance claim.

The omission is in the factory-shipped DB Skill itself (E49), not in an application-specific prompt or QA script. No factory template, injection configuration or build hook is needed to observe it: the Skill is the guidance artifact under review, and its transaction section is where the SQLite blocking warning and example would belong. No counter-evidence in the frozen factory materials shows another prompt supplying that warning.

The existing public guidance does not already cover this: the DB Skill's transaction section stops at rollback semantics (E49), and the application-development database-connections reference covers SQLite paths and configuration but not single-connection blocking or acquire timeouts (E75). The SQLite transaction patch protects COMMIT failure state only (E51), not a nested outer read. Searches of the frozen skills and the db-sqlite package found no documented pool or blocking guidance, so the improvement is not already available through an existing entry point.

findings.title: C01 reminder acceptance was blocked by absent queue data and a 24-hour SLA
findings.detail: Verify-3 verified the main flow, role isolation, notification click-through and dashboard metrics, but blocked C01 because the archived application had zero tickets, no authorized engineers, and a Normal SLA of 24 hours, so the overdue reminder could not be triggered inside the run. The task requested sample data.
findings.impact: The reviewer cannot confirm the 24-hour reminder end-to-end even though the application registers an overdue scan through the supported jobs API.
findings.suggestedChange: Seed at least one open/unassigned ticket and one authorized engineer before acceptance, and provide a controllable clock or shortened SLA for the reminder window.

diagnosis.trigger: Run C01 acceptance on a fresh snapshot.
diagnosis.expected: Deterministic sample tickets and roles plus a way to advance past the 24-hour threshold so the reminder is observable.
diagnosis.actual: Zero tickets, no authorized engineers and a real 24-hour SLA made the reminder untestable within the run.
diagnosis.workaround: Create tickets/roles manually and temporarily shorten the SLA or advance the clock.
diagnosis.acceptance: With seeded queue data and an accelerated clock/SLA, the overdue scan creates a manager notification and C01 can be completed.

findings.title: Authorization composes collection policies and record scopes without bespoke enforcement
findings.detail: The package resolves permission-set grants into database conditions, refuses absent policies, and exposes a repository withPolicy enforcement point. Users composes those invariants into account disable/delete transactions.
findings.impact: Applications can implement role-scoped ticket access without duplicating authorization logic.
findings.suggestedChange: Keep the collection-id policy contract and the explicit missing-policy denial as the documented pattern.

findings.title: In-app inbox provides durable user isolation and typed deep-link targets
findings.detail: The server store scopes every operation by user id and persists a validated target; the client exposes unread count, pagination, read-state mutations and target-bearing items. The application only composes its own page and bell.
findings.impact: Notifications remain authoritative across reconnects and can open the exact business record without custom delivery logic.
findings.suggestedChange: Retain the explicit target contract and user-scoped store as the public integration boundary.

findings.title: Client application provides route, service and i18n composition in one root
findings.detail: AppClientRoot mounts the router and Refine, while AppClientProviders composes React providers, navigation guards and route contributions. API, i18n, breadcrumb and toaster services are exported for application pages.
findings.impact: Applications can add pages, route authorization and translations without rebuilding the shell or service wiring.
findings.suggestedChange: Continue exposing these composition points as stable public entries.

findings.title: Jobs service exposes per-scope schedule executors for quiet reminders
findings.detail: getScheduleExecutor(scope, name) caches by selection key and scope, the app-server provider registers jobExecutorServiceToken, and the scheduler skill directs non-UI tasks to this API rather than the admin-facing Scheduler plugin.
findings.impact: The application can implement the overdue scan as background work without adding an unnecessary administrator task UI.
findings.suggestedChange: Keep the per-scope executor API and the explicit Scheduler-versus-executor decision rule.

evidence.observation: Authorizer converts an unrestricted decision into a conditional database policy with a collection id, fields and scope true. The UNRESTRICTED_ACCESS message is a reason attached to a permitted result, not a denial.
Authorization registers an authenticated subject and adds {type:'authenticated', id:'*'} to every request. This supports default access for signed-in users without inventing a role.
Repository withPolicy normalizes the supplied policy and refuses an absent policy instead of silently running unscoped. This is the enforcement point for record-scoped service queries.

Users management runs disable/remove inside a caller-owned transaction and asks the Permission Sets API whether a subject is still removable. It composes user administration with permission-set invariants.

The Users guidance states that the plugin contributes only the invitation page and no user-management page, and that the application must build it on UsersClient. It also states the plugin grants no access by itself.
evidence.excerpt:
- Client registration factory and `UsersClientOptions`:
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/client`. It contributes only the public
  invitation page at `/invite/:token`; there is no user management page.
- Typed API client: `UsersClient` and its types from
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/client/user-client`.
- Server contracts: `userManagementServiceToken`,
  `userRoleScopeRegistryToken`, `UserRoleScope`, and related types from
  `@nocobase/app-plugin-users/server/tokens`.
- HTTP API: `GET /api/users` (`page`, `pageSize`, `q`, `status`, `roleScope`, `role`; answers `{ data, meta: { page, pageSize, total } }`), `GET /api/users/options`, `POST /api/users`, `PATCH /api/users/:userId`, `DELETE /api/users/:userId?confirm=true`, `POST /api/users/:userId/disable|enable|resetPassword|revokeSessions`, and `PUT /api/users/:userId/roleScopes/:scope`. The running application documents each one, with request and response schemas, at `/api/swagger/docs` (JSON at `/api/swagger`) under the `Users` tag. Failures use the standard error body; branch on `error.reason`, such as `USER_NOT_FOUND`, `SELF_DELETE_NOT_ALLOWED`, `LAST_ASSIGNMENT` or `USER_EMAIL_CONFLICT`.

Every HTTP route requires Authentication and Authorization. Routes check the `user` record type with one of `read`, `create`, `update`, `disable`, `enable`, `assign-role`, `reset-password`, `revoke-sessions` or `delete`. Account creation checks both `create` and `assign-role`. `delete` is permitted only while an application role scope can clean a deleted user up.

## Register the plugin

1. Register Authentication, Authorization, and then Users in the App's Client
   and Server plugin arrays. The Client factory takes no placement options:
   `users()`.
2. Grant only the `user` actions those roles need, on `{ type: 'user', id: '*' }` because `user` is a record type. The plugin creates no roles and grants no access by itself.
3. For a user management page, build it in the App on `UsersClient` and declare it among the App's own routes with the page access it needs; the plugin ships none.

evidence.observation: The business-module example authorizes a composite action, reads decision.conditions.database, indexes it by collection name (quotes, projects), and binds each policy to its repository. The keying contract is unambiguous.
File upload action configuration only accepts a positive maxSize; no extension, MIME or content allowlist is part of the route configuration.
The upload route checks multipart content type and that a File is present, then stores it. It performs no magic-byte or MIME allowlist check.
The repository normalizes filename/extension, stores the browser-supplied MIME after validMime, verifies stored size, and creates metadata. There is no content sniffing step.

The File skill defines upload defaults and explicitly says the plugin has no built-in content sniffing or malware scan; applications must implement business validation. This makes corrupt-content acceptance an application responsibility.
evidence.excerpt:
- Upload defaults are 5 MiB single / 20 MiB batch for the whole multipart body, including overhead. Direct Server uploads have no HTTP limit; UI maxSize checks an individual file. The Client supplies the multipart boundary.
- Upload failures use the standard `/api` error body with domain `file`; branch on `error.reason` (`ApiClientError.reason` in the Client), never on `message`. A successful upload answers 201.
- BODY_TOO_LARGE (413) and UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE (415): reduce request size or adjust route limits; send `multipart/form-data`. INVALID_MULTIPART/INVALID_FILE/INVALID_FILES (400): send native File values and a nonempty batch. PRINCIPAL_REQUIRED (403): a Policy function needs a resolved principal.
- INVALID_FILE_COLLECTION: first compare the migration name, route collection and Server repository argument; then await collections.get(logicalName) and check the active connection and generated metadata. SQLite physical text does not imply a broken datetime definition. Fix the specific lookup, metadata or schema problem and retry the same upload; do not bypass File Repository. Use a new migration for corrections to already-merged history.
- STORAGE_URL_UNAVAILABLE (503): configure a capable disk or stream mode.
- FILE_COMMIT_UNCERTAIN / FILE_CLEANUP_FAILED: reconcile database records and stored objects before retrying; uploads have no idempotency key.

There is no built-in route authentication, row ACL, Range/206, ETag, conditional download, resumable upload, physical cleanup, content sniffing or malware scan. Metadata deletion retains objects; cancelled forms may leave unlinked files. Implement the policies required by the business, including referenced-file deletion and orphan cleanup.

evidence.observation: The DB transaction guidance warns that outer db.query()/repository()/connection() calls inside a transaction do not roll back. It does not warn that on a single-connection SQLite pool such a call blocks until the pool acquire timeout and looks like a hung request.
SQLite configurePool only wraps afterCreate for decimal aggregates; it does not set pool size or an acquire timeout. The single-connection default therefore remains in force.
SQLite patches COMMIT failure so a pooled connection is rolled back before release. This protects transaction state but does not address a nested read waiting for the same single connection.

Scheduler guidance says non-UI recurring tasks should use an application-owned ScheduleExecutor from jobExecutorServiceToken, not the Scheduler plugin. This matches the quiet overdue reminder requirement.
evidence.excerpt:
## Decide Whether to Use Scheduler

The primary reason to define tasks through Scheduler is **UI observability for business administrators**. Developers define schedules and execution logic in code. Business administrators use the task list and detail pages the application builds on the Scheduler API to view schedules, track individual executions, and enable or disable tasks when authorized.

Tasks that do not need to be viewed and tracked through the UI must not be managed by the Scheduler plugin. Give recurring ones a `ScheduleExecutor` of their own from the application's jobs service (`jobExecutorServiceToken` in `@nocobase/app-server/jobs`), and one-off background work a `JobExecutor`; the application development Skill describes both. For administrator-visible tasks, deliver Client registration, access permissions, meaningful task names, and accurate final execution status together; successful server-side dispatch alone is incomplete.

evidence.observation: The jobs service exposes getScheduleExecutor(scope, name), caches executors by selection key and scope, and resolves memory or Redis backends. Per-scope scheduled work is a first-class API.
The app-server jobs provider registers jobExecutorServiceToken and creates the executor service from application jobs config, giving application services a supported way to schedule background work.
The client package exports the application, router/providers, API client, route contributions with auth/authz metadata, i18n runtime, breadcrumb and toaster services.

AppClientRoot mounts the browser router and Refine providers; AppClientProviders composes React providers, navigation guards and route contributions. This is the supported page/routing composition layer.

The i18n guidance says not to build a language picker because the template already renders one, and explains namespace scope for application pages. Translation support is supplied rather than reimplemented.
evidence.excerpt:
- Do not build a language picker. `useAppLocale()` exists; `app-template-default` already renders one in `client/layouts/components/language-switcher.tsx`.
- Do not add i18n machinery to an application. The plugin is registered by default, the client runtime is built by `createAppI18nRuntime`, and the server's by `I18nProvider`.
- Do not configure the list of languages. It is whatever the application's own `locales/index.ts` declares; configuration names only the default, `i18n.defaultLocale` (overridden by `APP_DEFAULT_LOCALE`). The `@nocobase/app-plugin-i18n` README covers that, `useAppLocale()`, the endpoints, and `useSyncServerLocale()`, which the template shell already calls to keep the server's language in step with the browser's.

# The one rule that decides everything

**A namespace is a package name, and the namespace in scope follows the render tree.**

An application's pages get the application's namespace; a plugin's pages get that plugin's, because the host wraps each contribution using the `packageName` it already records. So a component in its own package's routes translates with no namespace at all.

evidence.observation: The in-app notification skill states that the plugin owns persistence, APIs and client inbox components, while the application owns its page and route. It does not promise a header bell or a notifications page.
evidence.excerpt:
This Skill is published with `@nocobase/app-plugin-notification-in-app`. The plugin owns its Server runtime, persistence, APIs, realtime contract, and Client inbox components. The target application owns whether both Client and Server entries are registered.

# Scope

- Register the Client and Server plugin entries and the core notification dependency.
- Render the exported inbox components in an application-owned page.
- Consume the public realtime topic and event types from the `/realtime` package entry.
- Verify or diagnose inbox HTTP access, mutations, user isolation, and reconnect refresh.

# Non-Goals

- Do not replace durable notifications with transient browser toasts.
- Do not edit inbox tables directly or publish forged realtime events as notification state.
- Do not expect the plugin to contribute an inbox page; the application owns the route.

evidence.observation: The client API exposes inbox items with an optional target, unread count and read/unread/delete mutations. These are the primitives needed for a bell and click-through.
The client implementation calls the authenticated notificationInApp/messages endpoints, reads paginated data and unread counts, and mutates read state. The browser does not reconstruct an API base.
The server store scopes every list, unread count and mutation by userId, persists target, and keeps HTTP state authoritative. This supports user-isolated durable notifications.

evidence.observation: The application comment records the reopen-hang root cause: the manager lookup was moved after the transaction because a reader takes another connection while the transaction already holds the only SQLite connection.
The final seed assigns the employee Permission Set to the authenticated subject for every signed-in account, including accounts registered after installation.
The final service policy helper indexes decision.conditions.database by the real collection names serviceDeskTickets and serviceDeskComments, and denies when no policy is present.
The application-owned bell composes inbox hooks, an unread count, mark-read behavior and navigation to the stored target or /inbox. The plugin supplies the hooks, not the header component.
The new-ticket form enforces only file count and size before uploading. It does not set accept or validate extension, MIME or content, so corrupt and unsupported files reach the generic upload path.
The final dashboard renders total tickets, awaiting assignment, resolution rate and overdue cards, with workload rendered later in the same page.

policyFor builds a database.collection resource with the collection id and folds read/create/update/delete decisions. Database policy keys are therefore collection ids, not an arbitrary composite logical name.

The common db client builds the knex pool by calling the dialect's configurePool(config, config.pool ?? {}), or uses config.pool ?? {} directly. With SQLite's configurePool present and no pool in the application config, the wrapper supplies no size or acquire timeout of its own; the underlying knex SQLite defaults remain.

The application's only connection is SQLite with dialect, filename, schemaManagement and debug; it sets no pool, max connections or acquire timeout, so the default single-connection SQLite pool is what the application uses.

Verify-3 records the employee filling a reopen reason and clicking Reopen ticket, after which #1 returns to In progress with the reason in the activity log and the engineer is notified. This is the same reopen flow that Verify-2 saw hang, and it runs after the manager lookup was moved outside the transaction.

evidence.excerpt:
Start by reading `server/config/database.ts` and the connection structure in `config.example.yml`. The template's default connection is `main` on SQLite. Preserve other connections and driver registrations when changing one connection.

| Location                    | Responsibility                                                                                                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `server/config/database.ts` | Declare connection defaults with `defineAppDatabaseConfig`; optionally register explicit drivers; map environment variables.          |
| `config.yml`                | Override connection settings for the environment, including credentials. This file is gitignored.                                     |
| `config.example.yml`        | Document the supported connection structure and credential placeholders for future installations. Keep it aligned with code defaults. |

The callback passed to `defineAppDatabaseConfig` receives the runtime context and runs during configuration resolution, not at module import. When supplied, explicit drivers determine the accepted dialects and connection fields in TypeScript. Without registrations, use a driver-owned connection type with `satisfies` when strict dialect-specific checking is needed. YAML overrides are resolved at runtime; passing `pnpm typecheck` does not validate their contents or prove connectivity.

The second argument of `defineAppDatabaseConfig` declares the section's environment variables. The templates pass `{ env: connectionEnvironment('main') }`, which maps `DB_DIALECT`, `DB_HOST`, `DB_PORT`, `DB_DATABASE`, `DB_USERNAME`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_SSL` and `DB_FILENAME` onto `connections.main`, above `config.yml`. A connection you add declares its own with a prefix naming it, merged into the same `env`: `{ ...connectionEnvironment('main'), ...connectionEnvironment('analytics', 'DB_ANALYTICS') }`. For SQLite, a `database` alias in `config.yml` still takes precedence over `DB_FILENAME`.

`config.yml` deep-merges into code defaults. Changing a dialect in code does not remove an old YAML override or fields belonging to the previous dialect. Update both layers when switching, and check any existing environment overrides using the Configuration section of `README.MD` in the application root.

Official drivers are optional peers of `@nocobase/app-server`. Install the needed package in application `dependencies` and configure its dialect; no driver import or registration is required. The application runtime awaits `resolveDatabaseConfig()` after configuration and defaults are merged, before provider registration. It imports only configured dialects and does not open connections. The core manager stays synchronous and requires prepared or explicitly registered drivers. YAML cannot install packages. Explicit `drivers` and connection-level `databaseDriver` values retain precedence and conflict checking. Custom dialects require explicit registration; registration keys must match their driver's dialect.

### SQLite paths

TypeScript connections require `filename`, normally `runtime.paths.storage('database.sqlite')`. YAML also accepts `database: database.sqlite`: the SQLite driver resolves it under the application's storage directory. Absolute paths remain absolute, and `:memory:` is preserved.

The YAML `database` alias takes precedence over `filename` during normalization. If changing `filename` appears to have no effect, check for an existing `database` override. Use `filename` in typed code; the YAML alias is not part of `SqliteConnectionConfig`.
